source_evidence.anchor: equation (1) and its immediately following paragraph
source_evidence.observation: For n-by-n square matrices with exact product C=A·B, stable matrix multiplication means that the computed Ccomp satisfies ||Ccomp-C|| <= mu(n) epsilon ||A|| ||B|| + O(epsilon^2). Here epsilon is machine epsilon bounding roundoff, and mu(n) is a low-degree polynomial, mu(n)=O(n^c) for some constant c. The paper says norms may be exchanged at the cost of additional dimension-dependent factors.
Recursive triangular inversion partitions T into diagonal blocks T11 and T22 of size n/2 by n/2 and computes the off-diagonal inverse block as -T11^-1·T12·T22^-1.

source_evidence.anchor: paragraph beginning 'To show that this algorithm is logarithmically stable' and equation (8)
source_evidence.observation: The paper explicitly calls the analysis first order and calls err(T^-1,n) an absolute error. For C=A·B whose operands have inherited errors err(A,n) and err(B,n), it writes err(C,n)=mu(n)epsilon||A||||B||+||A||err(B,n)+err(A,n)||B||. The three displayed labels identify fresh matrix-multiplication error, amplification of B's error by ||A||, and amplification of A's error by ||B||.

source_evidence.anchor: paragraph and recurrences immediately following equation (8)
source_evidence.observation: The recursive application replaces n by n/2 for block products. For T11^-1·T12, only the inherited error in T11^-1 is propagated; for the subsequent multiplication by T22^-1, equation (8) contributes fresh multiplication error and inherited errors from both operands. The paper states that it arbitrarily chooses to premultiply T12 by T11^-1 first.

source_evidence.anchor: continuation of the Section 3.1 error recurrence
source_evidence.observation: The terms generated from equation (8) are combined with inequalities into a recurrence bounding err(n), confirming that the displayed first-order rule is used as error-bound accounting rather than as an all-orders identity for exact errors.

source_evidence.anchor: Section 3.2 paragraph beginning 'For the rest of this section'
source_evidence.observation: The paper explicitly declares the matrix norm to be the 2-norm only later, within Section 3.2. No corresponding norm identification accompanies equation (8) in Section 3.1.

binders: n is the matrix-size parameter appearing in err(·,n) and mu(n); equation (1) explicitly concerns n-by-n square multiplication, while the recursive uses of equation (8) have block size n/2. [PDF p. 2, eq. (1); PDF p. 8, recurrences after eq. (8)]

A and B are compatible matrix operands, and C=A·B is their intended exact product; their available computed values may already carry inherited errors err(A,n) and err(B,n). [PDF p. 8, sentence introducing eq. (8)]
Ccomp denotes the result computed by the matrix-multiplication algorithm in the cross-referenced stability model. [PDF p. 2, eq. (1)]
epsilon is machine epsilon and bounds roundoff error. [PDF p. 2, paragraph containing eq. (1)]
mu(n) is the dimension-dependent matrix-multiplication error factor, specified as a low-degree polynomial satisfying mu(n)=O(n^c) for some constant c. [PDF p. 2, paragraph following eq. (1)]
hypotheses: The multiplication algorithm obeys the normwise stability model ||Ccomp-A·B|| <= mu(n)epsilon||A||||B||+O(epsilon^2) for exact n-by-n operands. [PDF p. 2, eq. (1)]

The operands used in the current multiplication may be outputs of prior computations and therefore have inherited absolute normwise errors err(A,n) and err(B,n). [PDF p. 8, sentence introducing eq. (8)]
The analysis retains only first-order error contributions. [PDF p. 8, paragraph introducing eq. (8)]
A and B have dimensions compatible with C=A·B; equation (8) does not itself state more specific dimensions. [PDF p. 8, sentence introducing eq. (8)]

In the triangular-inversion application, the displayed inverses require T and its diagonal blocks to be invertible, although the passage does not separately quantify nonsingularity. [PDF p. 8, opening block-inverse identity]
conclusions: The first-order product-error accounting is err(C,n)=mu(n)epsilon||A||||B||+||A||err(B,n)+err(A,n)||B||. [PDF p. 8, eq. (8)]
The term mu(n)epsilon||A||||B|| is the fresh error contributed by the matrix-multiplication operation. [PDF p. 8, first annotation under eq. (8)]
The term ||A||err(B,n) propagates and amplifies the inherited error in B. [PDF p. 8, second annotation under eq. (8)]
The term err(A,n)||B|| propagates and amplifies the inherited error in A. [PDF p. 8, third annotation under eq. (8)]
definitions_and_conventions: The exact product is C=A·B, while Ccomp is its computed counterpart in equation (1). [PDF p. 2, eq. (1)]

The immediate Section 3.1 prose describes err(T^-1,n) as an absolute error, and the subsequent prose describes err(n') as a bound for normwise error; equation (8) uses the same err notation for products and inherited operand errors. [PDF p. 8, paragraphs surrounding eq. (8)]

First order means that the displayed accounting keeps fresh O(epsilon) roundoff and terms linear in each inherited error; higher-order interactions are suppressed. This interpretation is inferred from the explicit O(epsilon^2) remainder in equation (1), the words 'first order,' and the absence of such interactions from equation (8). [PDF p. 2, eq. (1); PDF p. 8, paragraph and eq. (8)]
The later recurrence uses err quantities as upper bounds, even though equation (8) is printed with an equals sign. [PDF p. 8, recurrences after eq. (8); PDF p. 9, continuation of the recurrence]
implicit_context: Equation (8) is introduced as the local propagation rule in the analysis of recursive triangular matrix inversion. [PDF p. 8, Section 3.1 opening and paragraph introducing eq. (8)]

The off-diagonal inverse block is formed from two successive products involving T11^-1, T12, and T22^-1; the paper chooses the parenthesization (T11^-1·T12)·T22^-1. [PDF p. 8, opening identity and note preceding the recurrences]

For the triangular-inversion recurrence, the paper additionally uses ||Tii|| <= ||T||, ||Tii^-1|| <= ||T^-1||, and kappa(Tii)=||Tii||||Tii^-1|| <= kappa(T). These are application-specific facts, not extra terms in equation (8). [PDF p. 8, paragraph following eq. (8)]
statement.algorithm_linkage: Equation (8) supplies the local error rule for each matrix product in recursive triangular inversion. The diagonal blocks are recursively inverted, and the off-diagonal block is formed as -T11^-1·T12·T22^-1, with the paper choosing to compute T11^-1·T12 first and then multiply by T22^-1. [PDF p. 8, Section 3.1 opening identity and recurrences after eq. (8)]
numerical_model: Matrix multiplication is assumed to satisfy the normwise model of equation (1), with fresh roundoff bounded to first order by mu(n)epsilon||A||||B||. [PDF p. 2, eq. (1); PDF p. 8, eq. (8)]
epsilon is machine epsilon, described as bounding roundoff error. [PDF p. 2, paragraph containing eq. (1)]
mu(n) is polynomially bounded in n and depends on matrix size rather than on the particular operands in the displayed notation. [PDF p. 2, paragraph following eq. (1)]
Equation (8) extends the exact-input model by propagating errors already present in both operands. [PDF p. 8, sentence and annotations accompanying eq. (8)]
error_notions: The result concerns absolute normwise forward error in a computed product, not relative error or backward error. [PDF p. 8, paragraph introducing eq. (8)]
Fresh multiplication error and inherited input errors are distinct contributions. [PDF p. 8, annotations under eq. (8)]
Both inherited operand errors must be represented; neither is assumed zero in the general rule. [PDF p. 8, eq. (8)]
In the recursive application, err(n') denotes a bound valid for any encountered n'-by-n' diagonal subblock inverse. [PDF p. 8, paragraph following eq. (8)]
norms: The notation ||·|| denotes a matrix norm, but Section 3.1 does not identify a specific norm for equation (8). [PDF p. 8, eq. (8); PDF p. 10, later 2-norm declaration in Section 3.2]

The cross-referenced discussion says one may switch between finite-dimensional norms at the expense of additional n-dependent factors in the polynomial error constant. [PDF p. 2, paragraph following eq. (1)]
The triangular-inversion application uses monotonicity for diagonal submatrices, namely ||Tii|| <= ||T|| and ||Tii^-1|| <= ||T^-1||. [PDF p. 8, paragraph following eq. (8)]
constants_and_indexing: mu(n)=O(n^c) for some constant c and is characterized as a low-degree polynomial. [PDF p. 2, paragraph following eq. (1)]
Each of the three displayed first-order contributions in equation (8) has coefficient one apart from the factor mu(n) multiplying fresh roundoff. [PDF p. 8, eq. (8)]
When equation (8) is applied to n/2-by-n/2 recursive blocks, the fresh-error factor is mu(n/2), and inherited errors are indexed by n/2. [PDF p. 8, recurrences after eq. (8)]
No index offset such as n+1 or n-1 appears in the selected rule. [PDF p. 8, eq. (8)]
higher_order_terms: Equation (1) explicitly includes an O(epsilon^2) remainder. [PDF p. 2, eq. (1)]
Equation (8) is explicitly presented within a first-order analysis and displays no higher-order remainder. [PDF p. 8, paragraph and eq. (8)]

Under the first-order interpretation, products of inherited errors and interactions between fresh roundoff and inherited errors are omitted as higher-order effects; the paper does not enumerate these omitted terms. [PDF p. 2, eq. (1); PDF p. 8, first-order paragraph and eq. (8)]
exceptional_values: The cited numerical model states no handling assumptions for overflow, underflow, NaNs, or infinities; it mentions only machine epsilon as a roundoff bound. [PDF p. 2, paragraph containing eq. (1); PDF p. 8, paragraph containing eq. (8)]

The inversion application implicitly excludes singular T or singular diagonal blocks because T^-1, T11^-1, and T22^-1 occur in the displayed algorithm, but no separate exceptional-value clause is stated. [PDF p. 8, opening block-inverse identity]

undebatable_constraints: The selected rule must contain all three first-order contributions: fresh matrix-multiplication roundoff, propagation of B's inherited error, and propagation of A's inherited error. [PDF p. 8, eq. (8) and its annotations]
The fresh term must have the form mu(n)epsilon||A||||B||. [PDF p. 8, first line of eq. (8)]
B's inherited error must be multiplied by ||A||, and A's inherited error must be multiplied by ||B||. [PDF p. 8, second and third lines of eq. (8)]
The error notion is absolute and normwise in the Section 3.1 analysis. [PDF p. 8, paragraph introducing eq. (8)]

The rule is first-order accounting and must not be strengthened into an exact all-orders identity without a remainder or additional assumptions. [PDF p. 2, eq. (1); PDF p. 8, first-order paragraph; PDF p. 9, bounding recurrence]
The matrix-multiplication factor mu is dimension dependent and polynomially bounded, with mu(n)=O(n^c). [PDF p. 2, paragraph following eq. (1)]
The general rule permits inherited error in both operands, even though a particular recursive product may have one exact original-input operand. [PDF p. 8, eq. (8) and first product recurrence]
The local recursive applications use block-size argument n/2 and therefore mu(n/2), not mu(n), for n/2-by-n/2 products. [PDF p. 8, recurrences after eq. (8)]

ambiguities.issue: Equation (8) is printed with an equals sign although the surrounding analysis is about bounds.
ambiguities.evidence: The paper says 'we may write' and prints err(C,n)=... in equation (8), but immediately applies it through <= inequalities and calls err(n') a bound. [PDF p. 8, eq. (8) and following recurrences; PDF p. 9, continuation]
ambiguities.impact: A formalization should treat the expression as first-order error-bound accounting unless err is explicitly defined to equal the chosen bound; literal equality of actual errors would be stronger than the source.

ambiguities.issue: The particular matrix norm used in Section 3.1 is not named.
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (1) discusses changing norms, equation (8) uses generic ||·||, and an explicit 2-norm declaration appears only later in Section 3.2. [PDF p. 2, paragraph after eq. (1); PDF p. 8, eq. (8); PDF p. 10, Section 3.2 norm declaration]
ambiguities.impact: The contract does not justify hard-coding the spectral norm solely from equation (8); an abstract suitable norm or a separately justified norm specialization is faithful.

ambiguities.issue: The exact dimensions covered by equation (8) are left implicit.
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (1) explicitly defines stability for n-by-n square matrices, whereas the sentence introducing equation (8) only says 'two matrices C=A·B'; its local uses are square n/2 block products. [PDF p. 2, eq. (1); PDF p. 8, sentence introducing eq. (8) and following recurrences]
ambiguities.impact: The source directly supports the square-block setting used by the algorithm; a theorem for arbitrary rectangular dimensions requires an additional interpretation or generalized multiplication assumption.

ambiguities.issue: The paper does not formally define which omitted expressions comprise 'first order.'
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (1) has an O(epsilon^2) remainder, while the Section 3.1 prose says 'first order' and equation (8) omits products of inherited errors and other mixed terms without listing them. [PDF p. 2, eq. (1); PDF p. 8, paragraph and eq. (8)]
ambiguities.impact: It is faithful to omit quadratic and mixed error interactions, but an exact remainder bound or its constants cannot be recovered from the selected passage.

ambiguities.issue: The notation err(X,n) is not separately and formally defined for arbitrary intermediate products.
ambiguities.evidence: The passage explicitly calls err(T^-1,n) an absolute error, then uses err(A,n), err(B,n), and err(C,n) in equation (8), and later defines err(n') as a bound for diagonal-subblock inverse errors. [PDF p. 8, paragraphs surrounding eq. (8)]
ambiguities.impact: A formal target must choose whether err denotes an actual norm difference or a maintained upper bound; the subsequent recurrence supports the upper-bound reading.

ambiguities.issue: Universal quantifiers and hidden-constant dependencies are expressed only in prose.
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (1) defines stability for an algorithm on n-by-n matrices and specifies mu(n), but neither equation (1) nor equation (8) gives a formal quantifier order or the dependencies of the hidden O(epsilon^2) constant. [PDF p. 2, eq. (1); PDF p. 8, eq. (8)]
ambiguities.impact: A formalization should not introduce operand-dependent mu factors or claim uniform higher-order constants beyond what the paper states.

contract_plain_english: For a product C=A·B evaluated by a normwise stable matrix-multiplication routine, if the two operands already contain inherited errors, the paper's first-order absolute-error accounting has exactly three displayed contributions: mu(n)epsilon||A||||B|| from the new multiplication, ||A||err(B,n) from B's inherited error, and err(A,n)||B|| from A's inherited error. Higher-order interactions are suppressed. The rule is then applied at block size n/2 to the two products forming -T11^-1·T12·T22^-1 in recursive triangular inversion. [PDF p. 2, eq. (1); PDF p. 8, Section 3.1 and eq. (8)]
